subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: My Body Is a Compass — Four Cardinal Directions

tasks_in_class.description: Manu faces the rising Sun; fill: that direction is ___, left hand points ___ direction, right hand points ___ direction; which way is west?

time_bands.activity: Students stand and face the direction from which sunlight enters the classroom or, if indoors, face where the teacher says East is. The teacher leads a choral call-and-response: 'I face East — my left is North, my right is South, behind me is West.' Students repeat while holding out their arms. The poem 'Four Little Chicks' from the textbook is read aloud in unison, with children miming each direction the chicks call out.

Students open their textbooks to p.171 and work through the Manu orientation task — p.171 ("Manu faces the rising Sun; fill: that direction is ___, left hand points..."). The teacher circulates and prompts: 'Stretch out your arms right now — which hand is North?' Students fill the blanks individually, then share answers with a neighbour and resolve any disagreement by physically re-enacting the body-compass stance.

Class-wide discussion: the teacher poses quick oral questions — 'If you face West, what is on your right? What is behind you?' — and cold-calls several students. A volunteer draws the four-direction cross on the board and labels it. Students check their own completed task against the board and correct errors in pencil.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is swapping North and South when the child faces West instead of East; prompt the child to re-enact the sunrise stance before answering any direction question. The poem 'Four Little Chicks' is a strong memory anchor — let children revisit it whenever they seem uncertain about a direction label.

section_titles: Bird Watching — Directions on a Camp Map
periods.activity_title: Tent Colours and Room Layouts — Directions on Maps

tasks_in_class.description: Read clues about tent positions (west of road, closest to lake, north of green, south of lake); colour tents accordingly; draw a tent east of the lake.
Write the directions of window, bed, cupboard, and bedside table in relation to the girl in the room diagram.

homework.description: Make a drawing of your room; locate directions of things from the centre; draw the direction arrow for your room.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the body-compass anchor built around facing the rising Sun and elicits the four directions from the class by cold-calling. Students rehearse the stance once more — arms out, naming each cardinal point — to prime spatial reasoning for map work.

Students open to Bird Watching!, p.172. The teacher reads the four directional clues aloud one at a time, pausing after each so students can identify which tent is described and colour it. Pairs discuss: 'How did you know that tent is west of the road and not east?' After colouring, students draw the new tent east of the lake and compare placement with a neighbour.

Students move to Map of a Room, p.172. The teacher orientates the class by pointing out the direction arrow on the diagram, then students individually write the cardinal direction of each object — window, bed, cupboard, bedside table — relative to the girl. The teacher asks two or three students to share their answers and justifies each with 'The arrow shows North is at the top of the map, so…'

Teacher sets the room-drawing homework from Map of a Room, p.173 and demonstrates quickly on the board: draw a rectangle, place a dot at the centre, draw the four-direction cross, and label one object in each direction. Students note what is needed so they can do this at home.

periods.teacher_notes: The key conceptual shift in the Bird Watching task is that North is now 'up on the map', not tied to the student's own body — many children initially rotate the book to face what feels like East; redirect them to use the printed compass rose. In the room diagram task, a common error is naming direction relative to the child's current seat rather than relative to the girl standing at the map's centre.

periods.activity_title: My Room on Paper — Personal Maps with Direction Arrows

tasks_in_class.description: Make a drawing of your room; locate directions of things from the centre; draw the direction arrow for your room.
Write the names of things placed in East, West, North, and South directions in your room.

time_bands.activity: The teacher models on the board how to draw a room outline as a rectangle, mark its centre, draw the four-direction cross rooted there, and place one item (e.g., 'door') in the correct direction. Students ask questions before starting their own. The teacher emphasises: 'Your direction arrow must show which way is North in your real room — think about where the Sun rises when you look out your window.'

Students create their own room maps on plain paper using Map of a Room, p.173 as a guide — drawing the room outline, placing objects, drawing the direction arrow. The teacher circulates, checking that each child's compass rose is present and that objects are placed in the quadrant that matches their stated direction. Students who finish early add more objects or decorate the map.

Students complete the listing task from Map of a Room, p.173 — writing object names under each cardinal heading (East, West, North, South) based on their own map. Pairs swap maps, cross-check each other's list against the drawn positions, and flag any mismatch. The teacher closes by asking two volunteers to share one surprising or tricky placement from their room.

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes orient their room map to match the book's picture rather than their actual room; ask each child 'Which wall does the morning Sun hit?' as a grounding check. The room-map activity deliberately connects personal space to abstract directional language — value all reasonable placements provided the direction arrow is consistent with the object list.

section_titles: Zoo Trip — Street Map and Bus Route
periods.activity_title: Reading Streets — Navigate the Zoo Bus Route

tasks_in_class.description: Fill blanks: bus goes north from parking, turns right onto ___ Road driving ___ direction to reach S1; turns right/left onto ___ Road driving ___ direction to reach S2.
(a) Houses east of Jaideep's; (b) route from Ravi's house to children's park; (c) stop closer to Lali's house; (d) route for Golu to nearest stop; (e) direction for Prem to reach Stop 2.

time_bands.activity: Teacher projects or sketches a simplified street grid on the board and asks: 'If I face North and turn right, which direction am I now facing?' After a quick choral response, the teacher orients the class to the street map on p.174 — pointing out the compass rose, the road names, the house positions, and the two bus stops. Students identify Hospital Road, Market Road, and Park Road before any questions are attempted.

Students work individually on Bus Route, p.174 — the blank-filling route trace ('bus goes north from parking, turns right onto ___ Road…'). The teacher pauses the class after the first blank to model: 'I put my pencil at the parking lot, I travel north — now I meet a road and turn right; right when facing north is East; so I am now travelling East on Hospital Road.' Students then complete the remaining blanks independently.

Students tackle the five sub-questions of Bus Route, p.174 — ("(a) Houses east of Jaideep's…") in pairs. The teacher circulates and listens to pair discussions. After pairs have attempted all five, a whole-class share-out covers one question per pair, with the teacher drawing the route on the board sketch for visual confirmation. Any disagreements are resolved by returning to the map's compass rose.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error in street-map navigation is conflating 'turn right' with 'face right on the page'; anchor every turn to the compass direction the bus is currently facing before applying the turn. For the five sub-questions, children may confuse 'closest stop' with 'stop to the north' — prompt them to measure or count road segments rather than guess by visual impression.

periods.activity_title: Decoding the Metro Map — Lines, Legends, and Routes

tasks_in_class.description: Read the key; identify symbols on the metro map; name what different coloured lines represent; mark Qutb Minar on Yellow Line and Supreme Court on Blue Line.
(a) Trace different routes Qutb Minar→Supreme Court; (b) Lali's suggestion — which stations to change line again; (c) route with least stations; (d) best route to zoo from Qutb Minar.

time_bands.activity: Teacher holds up (or draws) a simple colour-coded key with three imaginary lines and asks: 'How would you know which line to take?' This bridges to the Delhi Metro map on p.175. Students read the key together — each coloured line is named aloud: Red, Yellow, Blue, Green, Violet, Pink, Magenta, Airport Express. Students then scan the map and mark Qutb Minar on the Yellow Line and Supreme Court on the Blue Line as directed by Delhi Metro Train Stations, p.175 ("Read the key; identify symbols…").

Students work in groups of three on Delhi Metro Train Stations, p.176 ("(a) Trace different routes Qutb Minar→Supreme Court…"). Each group traces as many routes as they can find with a finger on the map, then selects the route with the fewest stations and the route with the fewest line changes. Groups record their chosen routes with station names. The teacher listens to group reasoning: 'How many stations on this route? How many interchanges?'

Groups share findings. The teacher writes two or three proposed routes on the board as lists of station names and the class votes on 'best route to the zoo' — counting stations aloud together. The teacher closes by asking: 'What does the legend help us do that we could not do without it?' Students answer in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes trace routes without noting line changes; ask each group to circle every interchange station in pencil so it becomes visible when counting. The question of which route is 'best' is genuinely open — value any route where the student can state a clear criterion (fewest stations, fewest changes) and count consistently.

periods.activity_title: Build a School Map — Symbols, Keys, and Hidden Finds

tasks_in_class.description: Make a map of school with key for symbols; hide objects; mark positions with red dots/flags; challenge friends to find hidden things using the map.

time_bands.activity: The teacher discusses how the Delhi Metro legend uses simple shapes and colours to represent real stations and lines, and asks: 'Could we make a legend for our school building?' Students brainstorm which spaces matter — classroom, toilet, staircase, canteen, playground — and agree on a simple symbol for each. The teacher records three or four agreed symbols on the board as the class key.

In pairs, students draw a top-down sketch of the school — or the school floor they know — on plain paper, using the agreed symbols and adding their own additional ones to a key they draw in a corner. One partner then places a small sticker or pencil mark (the 'hidden object') at a chosen location on the map and marks it with a red dot. The other partner is not shown where it is yet.

Pairs swap maps. Using only the map and its key, the finder traces the route to the red dot and tries to name the real-school location. Partners then confirm or correct by comparing maps side by side. The teacher asks two pairs to share how useful their key was and what they would change — linking this back to the Delhi Metro map's legend as a model of a 'good key'.

periods.teacher_notes: If the school layout is complex, restrict the map to one floor or the immediate outdoor area so the map remains manageable within the time available. A common gap is a map with symbols but no key — remind students that the finder must be able to use the map without asking the maker any questions.
materials: Plain drawing paper (one sheet per pair)
Coloured pencils or stickers for marking hidden objects

section_titles: Anthill in the Zoo — Grid Distances and Directions
periods.activity_title: The Ant's Journey — Distance, Direction, and Shortest Paths

tasks_in_class.description: Fill blanks: distance and direction for ant to reach sugar (b), bread (c — two segments), apple (d — three segments); identify other routes to apple and which is shortest.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a simple 4×4 grid on the board and places a dot labelled 'anthill' at the lower-left corner. She places a 'sugar cube' two units to the right and asks: 'How would I tell the ant how to get there using direction and distance?' Students suggest answers; teacher models 'crawl 2 cm East' and writes it. Students open to Anthill in the Zoo, p.177 and identify the anthill and each food item.

Students work individually on Anthill in the Zoo, p.177 ("Fill blanks: distance and direction for ant to reach sugar (b), bread (c — two segments), apple (d — three segments)…"). The teacher circulates, checking that each segment is recorded as a distance-then-direction pair, and prompts students who are stuck on multi-segment paths to trace the route with their finger and count grid squares one direction at a time.

The open-ended part: students sketch or describe at least one alternative route to the apple and mark the total distance for each route. The class discusses which route is shortest by adding up the centimetre segments. The teacher asks: 'Can a longer-looking path on the map actually be shorter in distance?' to prompt reflection on route comparison.

periods.teacher_notes: Children frequently record direction before distance rather than distance-then-direction; consistently model the format '2 cm East' rather than 'East 2 cm' so that symbolic recording is uniform. For the alternative-route question, accept any valid path that stays on the grid; the goal is reasoning about total distance, not a unique answer.

periods.activity_title: Zoo Coordinates — Reading and Writing Ordered Pairs

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo), p.178
tasks_in_class.description: Fill blanks to reach tortoise: steps east→column, steps north→row; state location of tortoise (4,1); identify what is at (1,4).

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q1, p.178
tasks_in_class.description: Locate the animal at positions (11,11), (2,6), (6,4), (3,10), (11,3), (10,9) on the zoo grid map.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q2, p.178
tasks_in_class.description: Write the ordered-pair position of Lion, Elephant, Tortoise, Deer, Panda, and Crocodile on the zoo map.

homework.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q3, p.178
homework.description: Place coloured dots at positions (8,3) Red, (2,9) Green, (7,3) Blue, (3,8) Orange, (8,6) Black, (6,6) Pink on the zoo grid.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a small 5×5 grid on the board with numbered columns (1–5 left to right) and numbered rows (1–5 bottom to top). She places a star at column 3, row 2, and models: 'I walk East 3 steps to reach column 3, then North 2 steps to reach row 2 — so this star is at (3,2). Horizontal always comes first.' Students then open to Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo), p.178 and attempt the tortoise-path fill-in (steps east, steps north; confirm tortoise is (4,1); identify (1,4)).

Students work individually on Q1, p.178 — locating the animals at six given coordinates ("Locate the animal at positions (11,11), (2,6), (6,4)…"). The teacher circulates, watching for the axis-swap error (column/row reversed). After Q1 is complete, students move to Q2, p.178 — writing the ordered pairs for Lion, Elephant, Tortoise, Deer, Panda, and Crocodile.

Pairs compare Q1 and Q2 answers, reading each coordinate aloud: 'I said Lion is at (5,8) — I walked 5 steps East then 8 steps North.' The teacher selects one or two disagreements and works them out on the board grid. The class confirms or corrects. Homework task Q3, p.178 is set and briefly explained: students will colour dots at given coordinates on the zoo grid at home.

periods.teacher_notes: The most persistent error in coordinate reading is reversing the pair — writing (row, column) instead of (column, row); reinforce the rule 'East first, North second' using the physical act of walking: 'Slide along the bottom, then climb up.' Q1 and Q2 are complementary tasks (one gives coordinates, the other asks for them) — both are retained because one acts as verification for the other, a genuine cognitive gain rather than mere repetition.

periods.activity_title: Maps All the Way — From Body-Compass to Coordinate Grid

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses a quick whole-class oral quiz: 'Face East — what is on your left? What is behind you?' Then: 'On a map, North is at the top — you colour a tent west of the road; which side of the road do you colour?' Students answer chorally or are cold-called. This warm-up threads together body-anchored cardinal directions and map-top direction reading, both central themes of the chapter.

Students receive a teacher-drawn synthesis sheet (or use plain paper): a simple street map with four named roads, a compass rose, three house symbols, and a bus-stop marker. Working in pairs, students answer three questions the teacher writes on the board: (1) Name the house north-east of the bus stop. (2) The bus travels south on Road A and turns right — which road and direction does it now face? (3) Write the ordered pair for the house at column 4, row 3 on a grid overlay the teacher adds to the sketch. Questions span street-map reading, turn-and-direction reasoning, and coordinate notation — the three symbolic layers the chapter built.

Teacher draws a scaled grid on the board (5×5, 1 cm per unit). She places a flag at (2,3) and asks students to describe the shortest ant-path from (1,1) to the flag in direction-distance language. Students write their answer individually: '1 cm East, 2 cm North' or equivalent multi-segment routes. Two volunteers share their route and the class compares total distances, recalling that the grid-centimetre language comes from the anthill activity and checking whether a one-segment or two-segment path is shorter in this case.

Whole-class reflection: teacher asks, 'We started by using our own body as a compass and ended by giving a location as two numbers — how did each step change what we needed to know?' Students share one idea each in a quick round. The teacher summarises on the board: Body → Pictorial map → Street map with compass → Legend and key → Grid distance-direction → Ordered pair — a visible chain of the chapter's journey from concrete orientation to symbolic coordinate.

periods.teacher_notes: The synthesis sheet should be freshly drawn or printed for this unit — it requires no earlier student artefact and the questions are designed so that the concepts of cardinal direction, map reading, street navigation, and coordinate pairs are all exercised on a single new context. Watch for students who can read coordinates but revert to body-stance confusion when asked about map directions — this conflation is the chapter's deepest misconception and the closing discussion is the right moment to surface and resolve it.
materials: Teacher-prepared synthesis map sheet (plain paper, one per pair) OR plain paper for students to sketch on

items.prompt: A metro map has a key that shows: Red line = Dilshad Garden to Rithala, Blue line = Dwarka to Vaishali, Yellow line = HUDA City Centre to Samaypur Badli. Priya wants to travel on the Yellow line. Which symbol should she look for on the map?

options.label: A
options.text: A red-coloured line on the map

options.label: B
options.text: A yellow-coloured line on the map

options.label: C
options.text: A blue-coloured line on the map

options.label: D
options.text: Any coloured line — the colour does not matter

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A yellow-coloured line on the map
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the route name in the key to the colour shown beside it, then find that colour on the map.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have read the first line in the key (Red) without matching the key entry to the route name Priya wants.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have read the last key entry (Blue) without cross-checking which line name corresponds to Yellow.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student does not yet understand that a map legend assigns a unique colour to each line, making colour the identifying symbol.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student point to each key colour and say its line name aloud; stretch: ask them to design a two-line key for an imaginary tram system.

exercise.description: Read the key; identify symbols on the metro map; name what different coloured lines represent; mark Qutb Minar on Yellow Line and Supreme Court on Blue Line.

items.prompt: Draw a simple map key for a park. Your key must include symbols for: a tree, a drinking-water tap, and a toilet. Draw the symbol you choose for each and write its name beside it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any clearly drawn, distinct symbol for each feature (e.g., a triangle for tree, a circle with a drop for tap, a square for toilet) with the correct label written next to each symbol.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Choose a simple, distinct shape or picture for each real-world feature and pair it with its label to make a key.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student trace or copy the Delhi Metro key format from their textbook as a model; stretch: add a fourth symbol (e.g., a bench) and explain why their chosen symbol is easy to recognise.

exercise.description: Make a map of school with key for symbols; hide objects; mark positions with red dots/flags; challenge friends to find hidden things using the map.

items.prompt: Reena stands facing the rising Sun. She stretches both arms out to the sides. Which direction does her right hand point?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Face East (rising Sun); left arm = North, right arm = South, behind = West.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have confused left and right, assigning North to the right hand instead of the left.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may think the hand points in the same direction as the face, not understanding that the body is the compass with arms pointing perpendicular to the facing direction.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have reversed the rule completely, placing West on the right side.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to stand up, stretch arms, and physically re-enact facing the rising Sun before answering; stretch: ask what direction Reena's right hand would point if she turned to face North.

exercise.description: Manu faces the rising Sun; fill: that direction is ___, left hand points ___ direction, right hand points ___ direction; which way is west?

items.section_title: Bird Watching — Directions on a Camp Map
items.prompt: Look at the camp map in your textbook (Bird Watching!, p.172). The green tent is already placed on the map. A new red tent must be placed north of the green tent and west of the lake. Write one sentence explaining how you know exactly where to place the red tent.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The red tent goes in the spot that is directly above (north of) the green tent and to the left (west) of the lake — where both clues are satisfied at the same time.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use each directional clue to narrow the possible positions one at a time until only one spot satisfies all clues.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw a compass rose on the map corner and use it to check 'north' and 'west' one clue at a time; stretch: ask the student to write a third directional clue that would still describe the same tent position.

exercise.description: Read clues about tent positions (west of road, closest to lake, north of green, south of lake); colour tents accordingly; draw a tent east of the lake.

items.prompt: In a room map, the direction arrow shows North at the top. A student stands in the centre of the room. The door is to her right when she faces North. In which direction is the door?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Facing North: right side is East, left side is West.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may think 'in front' and 'right' are the same when facing North.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may have confused right with behind (South).
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have confused right and left, placing the door to the West instead of East.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student stand and face the classroom's North wall and physically identify which hand is East; stretch: ask the student to state the direction of the door if the student turned to face South instead.

exercise.description: Write the directions of window, bed, cupboard, and bedside table in relation to the girl in the room diagram.

items.section_title: Zoo Trip — Street Map and Bus Route
items.prompt: A bus starts at a parking lot and drives North along Elm Road. It then turns right onto Oak Road. In which direction is the bus now travelling? Write your answer and explain how you worked it out.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The bus is now travelling East. When you face North and turn right, you face East.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the body-compass rule: facing North, a right turn means the new facing direction is East.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to physically face the classroom's North wall and turn right — then name the direction they face; stretch: ask what direction the bus faces if it turns right again at the next junction.

exercise.description: (a) Houses east of Jaideep's; (b) route from Ravi's house to children's park; (c) stop closer to Lali's house; (d) route for Golu to nearest stop; (e) direction for Prem to reach Stop 2.

items.prompt: Arjun wants to travel from Station P to Station Q on a metro map. Route 1 passes through 6 stations and requires 1 line change. Route 2 passes through 4 stations and requires 2 line changes. Which route has fewer stations? Which route has fewer line changes? Which route would you call 'better' and why?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Route 2 has fewer stations (4 vs 6). Route 1 has fewer line changes (1 vs 2). Either route can be called better depending on the criterion chosen — Route 2 if fewer stations matters more; Route 1 if fewer changes matters more. Both answers are correct if the student states a clear reason.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count stations along each route and count line changes separately, then choose a criterion to compare.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a simple two-route diagram on paper and ask the student to count and circle stations; stretch: ask the student to suggest a third criterion (e.g., travel time) that might make a different route 'best'.

exercise.description: (a) Trace different routes Qutb Minar→Supreme Court; (b) Lali's suggestion — which stations to change line again; (c) route with least stations; (d) best route to zoo from Qutb Minar.

items.section_title: Anthill in the Zoo — Grid Distances and Directions
items.prompt: An ant starts at a point on a grid. It crawls 3 cm East, then 2 cm North to reach a piece of bread. Write the ant's path in direction-distance language. Then describe one different route the ant could take to reach the same bread, and state whether your new route is shorter, longer, or the same total distance.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Original path: 3 cm East, then 2 cm North — total 5 cm. An alternative route: 2 cm North then 3 cm East — total 5 cm, the same distance. (Or: 1 cm East, 2 cm North, 2 cm East — also 5 cm.) Any valid grid path with the correct total is accepted.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Record each segment as distance-then-direction and add segment lengths to find the total.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student squared paper to draw the grid and trace both routes physically; stretch: ask whether there is any route on the grid that could reach the same point in fewer than 5 cm.

exercise.description: Fill blanks: distance and direction for ant to reach sugar (b), bread (c — two segments), apple (d — three segments); identify other routes to apple and which is shortest.

items.prompt: On a zoo grid, you move 5 steps East and then 3 steps North to reach the giraffe. What is the ordered pair for the giraffe's position?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (5, 3) — 5 steps East gives column 5; 3 steps North gives row 3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The first number in the pair is steps East (column); the second is steps North (row).

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student reversed the pair — they put row first and column second, a common axis-swap error.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have used the East steps for both numbers in the pair.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have used the North steps for both numbers in the pair.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to say 'East first, North second' aloud and trace the steps on a small drawn grid before writing the pair; stretch: ask the student to write the ordered pair for an animal 2 steps North and 7 steps East.

exercise.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo), p.178
exercise.description: Fill blanks to reach tortoise: steps east→column, steps north→row; state location of tortoise (4,1); identify what is at (1,4).

items.prompt: The direction arrow on a room map shows North at the top. List one object you would expect to find in each of the four directions — North, South, East, and West — in a typical classroom. (You may use: door, window, blackboard, cupboard, teacher's table.)

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any one object placed in each of the four directions is correct, provided the student does not assign the same object to two directions and uses only the listed items (or other real classroom objects). For example: North — blackboard, South — cupboard, East — window, West — door.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the North arrow on the map as reference and place each object in the quadrant it occupies relative to the room's centre.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw a simple rectangle (the room), mark North at the top, and then write one object name in each quarter; stretch: ask the student to write two objects per direction and draw a direction arrow consistent with the real classroom.

exercise.description: Write the names of things placed in East, West, North, and South directions in your room.

items.prompt: On a zoo grid, the elephant is at column 7, row 4. Which ordered pair correctly shows the elephant's position?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (7, 4) — column number (East steps) first, row number (North steps) second.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write column first and row second: (column, row) = (7, 4).

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student reversed the pair, placing row before column.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student used the column number for both positions in the pair.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student used the row number for both positions in the pair.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the rule '(East steps, North steps)' on a card and let the student refer to it while answering; stretch: ask the student to write the ordered pair for an animal at column 3, row 10, and explain the rule in their own words.

exercise.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q1, p.178
exercise.description: Locate the animal at positions (11,11), (2,6), (6,4), (3,10), (11,3), (10,9) on the zoo grid map.

items.prompt: On a zoo grid, the lion is 9 steps East and 5 steps North of the entrance. Write the lion's ordered pair as two numbers separated by a comma inside brackets.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: East steps = first number, North steps = second number: (9, 5).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to write E=9, N=5 first, then place them in order inside brackets; stretch: ask the student to write the ordered pair for a deer that is 3 steps further East and 2 steps further North than the lion.

exercise.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q2, p.178
exercise.description: Write the ordered-pair position of Lion, Elephant, Tortoise, Deer, Panda, and Crocodile on the zoo map.
